ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Neurology (neuromuscular) Consultation — Lou Gehrig

code.originalText: Neuromuscular neurology consultation with EMG and nerve conduction studies; results of MRI and blood tests; diagnosis and start of treatment

text.paragraph: Progressive weakness and loss of coordination over about a year in a 35-year-old professional baseball player, with hand wasting, widespread fasciculations, weakness of grip and left ankle dorsiflexion, brisk reflexes with spread and Hoffmann signs, and normal sensation. I am concerned about a motor neuron disease. Please evaluate with EMG and nerve conduction studies, exclude treatable mimics, and advise on diagnosis and care. [S]

list.item: Does he have amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, or a treatable mimic such as cervical myelopathy, multifocal motor neuropathy, or an inflammatory or metabolic myopathy?
What do the EMG and nerve conduction studies show, and which diagnostic criteria are met?
What disease-modifying treatment do you advise, and should genetic testing be done?
How should breathing, nutrition, speech and swallowing, and mobility be monitored, and when should we intervene?
How should we support his work, his mood and early planning for future care?

text.paragraph: Mr. Gehrig, a 35-year-old professional baseball player, is seen at the request of Dr. Hollister for about a year of progressive weakness and loss of coordination, beginning with a decline in his play and progressing to fumbling with buttons, tripping on curbs and a fall on the ice, with cramps and twitching. He stopped playing two weeks ago. He has no sensory symptoms, neck pain, eye symptoms, or trouble speaking, swallowing or breathing. He has had several concussions in his career without lasting symptoms. No family history of ALS or dementia is known to him. [S]
Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Henry Louis Gehrig was born on June 19, 1903, in the Yorkville section of Manhattan, New York, to Heinrich and Christina Gehrig, German immigrants. [D]

Three of his siblings died young: his sister Anna in September 1902 at about three months, his sister Sophie in the winter of 1906 of a combination of measles, diphtheria and bronchopneumonia, and a brother shortly after birth. [D]
He enrolled at Columbia University on a football scholarship in February 1921. [D]
He played first base for the New York Yankees and, on May 2, 1939, in Detroit, took himself out of the lineup after a then-record 2,130 consecutive games. [D]

In 1938 he batted .295, the first time under .300 since 1925, and his hitting fell off sharply in midsummer; he had an attack of lumbago and a badly jammed thumb that season. In the winter of 1938 to 1939 he lost his strength and collapsed while ice skating, in spring training 1939 he collapsed while putting on his uniform pants and his reflexes had slowed alarmingly, and at 35 he batted .143 in the first games of the 1939 season. [D]
His first neurological symptoms began in 1938, around the time of his 35th birthday. [D]
He had repeated head injuries, including concussions, during his playing career. [D]

text.paragraph: 5 later historical claims are omitted because they describe events after the index age. See the teaching note.

tr.td: Riluzole 50 mg oral tablet, one tablet by mouth twice daily, an hour before or two hours after meals
One tablet by mouth every 12 hours on an empty stomach

Progressive weakness and loss of coordination for about a year: fumbling with buttons and a bat, tripping on curbs, a fall on the ice in the winter, muscle cramps and twitching in the arms and thighs; no numbness, pain, double vision, or trouble speaking or swallowing. Examination: wasting of the hand muscles (left more than right), fasciculations in both arms and thighs, weakness of grip and of left ankle dorsiflexion, brisk reflexes with spread and a positive Hoffmann sign, normal sensation. Mixed upper and lower motor neuron signs; evaluation for motor neuron disease and its mimics begun, with neuromuscular neurology consultation booked
S — Synthetic presenting problem anchored to his documented decline in 1938 and 1939; superseded by the diagnosis.

Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, limb onset: progressive weakness for about a year with upper and lower motor neuron signs in the cervical and lumbosacral regions, and active and chronic denervation on EMG in the cervical, thoracic and lumbosacral regions with normal sensory nerve conduction; MRI of the brain and cervical spine and blood tests exclude mimics. Meets the Gold Coast criteria and the revised El Escorial category of clinically probable ALS. ALSFRS-R 42 and FVC 88% of predicted at diagnosis. Synthetic modern episode linked to his documented diagnosis
S — Synthetic modern diagnosis; the documented 1939 diagnosis is the anchor. EMG findings, scores and timing are synthetic.

list.item: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, limb onset (G12.21). Progressive motor weakness over about a year with upper and lower motor neuron signs in the cervical and lumbosacral regions, and EMG evidence of active and chronic denervation in three regions with normal sensory conduction and no conduction block. Cervical myelopathy and structural lesions are excluded by MRI; multifocal motor neuropathy by the absence of conduction block and the upper motor neuron signs; myopathy by the EMG pattern and the modest creatine kinase; and metabolic, paraproteinemic and infectious mimics by the blood tests. This meets the Gold Coast criteria and the revised El Escorial category of clinically probable ALS. ALSFRS-R 42 and FVC 88% of predicted. His past concussions do not change the diagnosis or treatment. [S]

text.paragraph: Data reviewed: Dr. Hollister's intake note. MRI of the brain and cervical spine last week: normal, with no cord compression or structural lesion. Calcium 9.4 mg/dL, vitamin B12 512 pg/mL, TSH 1.6 mIU/L, A1c 5.2%, creatine kinase 412 U/L; serum protein electrophoresis with immunofixation shows no monoclonal protein; HIV test negative. Seated FVC 4.62 L (90%) at intake. EMG and nerve conduction studies this morning: normal sensory responses; reduced motor amplitudes in the median and ulnar nerves with normal conduction velocities and no conduction block; fibrillation potentials, positive sharp waves, fasciculation potentials and large, unstable motor units in the cervical (biceps, first dorsal interosseous), thoracic paraspinal, and lumbosacral (tibialis anterior, vastus lateralis) regions; bulbar muscles not yet affected. [S]

list.item: Diagnosis of ALS given to him in person today, with time for questions and written information. [S]
Riluzole 50 mg twice daily, with ALT monthly for 3 months and then every 3 months. [S]
Genetic testing for ALS-associated genes with genetic counseling today; tofersen only if an SOD1 variant is found. [S]
Edaravone discussed as an option with modest evidence in a selected group of patients; he chose to begin with riluzole alone and revisit it. [S]
Multidisciplinary ALS clinic every 2 to 3 months: ALSFRS-R, seated FVC and maximal inspiratory pressure, weight and swallowing at every visit; cognitive and behavioral screening; PHQ-9. [S]

Noninvasive ventilation when FVC falls below 50% of predicted, maximal inspiratory pressure is weaker than -60 cmH2O, overnight oximetry shows desaturation, or orthopnea appears; supine FVC and overnight oximetry when values fall. [S]
Nutrition with the dietitian to hold weight; discuss gastrostomy early, while FVC is above 50%. [S]
Physical and occupational therapy for an ankle-foot orthosis, a cane, hand aids and home safety; early power wheelchair evaluation. [S]
Social work for work accommodations and benefits; psychology as he wishes; advance care planning early and revisited. [S]

Discussed with Dr. Hollister, who joined for the diagnosis conversation. Mr. Gehrig heard the result first, without family present, as he asked, and decided who else would be told and when. He agreed to start riluzole and to genetic testing. He decides who receives this note. [S]

Follow-up: Genetic counselor with the result in about four weeks. First full ALS clinic visit in about five weeks, then every 2 to 3 months; primary care with Dr. Hollister in step with the clinic. [S]
